facts.fact: Blender has no dedicated built-in camera-matching tool; practitioner tutorials point to third-party add-ons and standalone apps (fSpy, Simple Camera Match, Photo-Match Camera) for matching a camera to a photo.

fSpy is a standalone still-image camera matching app, described as the successor to the older BLAM add-on; its developer describes still-image camera matching as computing field of view and camera orientation from an image given vanishing points.
With only one discernible vanishing point, the focal length must be supplied by the user or guessed by trial and error when using fSpy-style still-image matching.
Simple Camera Match is a Blender extension where the user draws X, Y and Z vanishing lines over a background image in the camera viewport, and the add-on solves focal length, location and rotation.
Simple Camera Match guidance: pick orthogonal references such as building edges or box edges and draw the X, Y and Z lines along edges of each respective axis.

Photo-Match Camera is an archviz add-on for flat upright facades: the photo plane must stand upright, the camera is placed level with no tilt and no roll, and focal length is estimated from a known real-world width and camera distance.
Camera matching solvers need sensor size as well as focal length for a good solution; sensor-size and focal-length values in Blender have been questioned as inaccurate in a community thread.

A Blender Artists thread reports that the Blender viewport's focal length can appear to need roughly twice the camera focal length to match the camera view; a maintainer disputed this as a bug (per the thread summary). Treat as unconfirmed community report.

Poly Light Match is a Blender add-on that builds an image-based lighting rig from a reference photo, offering presets for movie, portrait, landscape and product shots, with controls for intensity, distance, height and rotation.

The Lightmap Blender tutorial 03 (Smart Car) matches an HDRI to a backplate photo by correcting HDRI orientation to the backplate, then refining the map by reducing light from under the tires and brightening the headlight reflection.
A Maya-based lighting course matches lighting to a reference by rotating the environment light until the light direction on the object matches the reference photo (not a Blender method).
In Blender, the Mix node Factor sets blend amount regardless of alpha, while Alpha Over respects the foreground alpha channel.
Blender compositing works in linear color, whereas After Effects blends in display space by default, so the same blend mode (e.g. difference) can give different results between the two.
After Effects limits blend modes to a layer's alpha by default, while Blender blend operations do not; black outside a layer can therefore affect a Blender result.
Blend modes are per-pixel formulas mixing foreground and background pixels; shaders only see the foreground, so background-dependent modes such as Overlay cannot be rebuilt inside a shader.

contradictions: Blender viewport vs camera focal length: a community report says the viewport needs about 2x the focal length to match, while a Blender maintainer disputed this as a bug (per the forum thread summary; not verified against the primary bug tracker).
Blender compositor vs After Effects: Blender Artists thread says results differ due to linear vs display color space and alpha limiting; no single authoritative resolution was retrieved.
